content: Bronchiolitis is a leading cause of respiratory failure in infants, and some cases necessitate intensive care and mechanical ventilation. Currently, there is limited evidence supporting treatments beyond supportive care for this condition. In severe cases of bronchiolitis, abnormalities in the quantity or quality of pulmonary surfactant have been observed. Administering exogenous surfactant has shown potential to improve lung function and may represent a promising therapeutic option for severe bronchiolitis. This review is an update of a previous publication from 2012, and no new studies were identified for inclusion, leaving the conclusions unchanged. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy of exogenous surfactant therapy, administered intratracheally (using either animal-derived or synthetic surfactant, at any dose and timing after ventilation initiation), in reducing mortality and the duration of mechanical ventilation in infants and children with bronchiolitis requiring mechanical ventilation. The search strategy included databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, LILACS, and Web of Science, covering studies up to June 2015. The inclusion criteria focused on prospective, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs evaluating the effects of exogenous surfactant in this patient population. Three small RCTs involving a total of 79 participants were included in the analysis. Two of these trials did not use a placebo in the control group, while the third trial employed an air placebo. None of the studies reported any mortality. The risk of bias was judged to be low or unclear across all categories for the included studies, with no study deemed to have a high risk of bias. The pooled analysis of the three trials showed no significant difference in the duration of mechanical ventilation between the surfactant and control groups (mean difference [MD] -63.04 hours, 95% confidence interval [CI] -130.43 to 4.35 hours). However, the duration of intensive care unit (ICU) stay was shorter in the surfactant group compared to the control group (MD -3.31 days, 95% CI -6.38 to -0.25 days). After excluding one trial that introduced significant heterogeneity, the results demonstrated a significant reduction in both the duration of mechanical ventilation (MD -28.99 hours, 95% CI -40.10 to -17.87 hours) and ICU stay (MD -1.81 days, 95% CI -2.42 to -1.19 days) in the surfactant group. Surfactant therapy also showed favorable effects on oxygenation and carbon dioxide elimination. Importantly, no adverse effects or complications were reported in any of the three included studies. The quality of evidence for outcomes such as duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU stay, oxygenation, and carbon dioxide parameters was rated as moderate. In conclusion, exogenous surfactant therapy demonstrated beneficial effects on the duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU stay, oxygenation, and carbon dioxide elimination in critically ill infants with bronchiolitis requiring mechanical ventilation. However, the small number of studies and participants (n = 79) limits the strength of the evidence. Larger, well-powered trials with cost-effectiveness analyses are needed to establish the efficacy and feasibility of surfactant therapy in this population.
